To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) contact electrification is an efficient way to generate attractive interactions between components that are identical in shape and size; (ii) the interactions are strong enough to assemble these components into ordered, macroscopic aggregates; (iii) the aggregates are highly ordered and possess a net electric charge; (iv) the charge is due to the formation of electric dipoles in the particles that are in contact with the charged particles in the aggregates; and (v) the dipoles induce attractive forces

1) macroscopic objects made of polymeric materials can be electrostatically assembled into ordered, closed structures, 2) the structures that form are not necessarily electroneutral, and 3) their stability can be explained by taking into account the interactions between electric dipole moments that the particles in an aggregate generate in their neighbours.

the self-assembly into ordered arrays of components of identical dimensions but with different electrical properties can be achieved by using the electrical interactions between these components that are generated by the process of contact electrification.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a simple, yet highly effective, approach to self-assemble macroscopic objects into highly ordered structures.
the self-assembly and the stability of binary, macroscopic crystals.
the assembly of two types of objects that are of equal size and shape but have different electrical properties.

the electrostatic self- assembly of macroscopic crystals is an important new technique for the construction of materials with a range of applications.

the self-assembly process is a consequence of the interplay of two different forces: electrostatic repulsion between like-charged particles and electrostatic attraction between unlike-charged particles.
